title: Batching priority inversion postmortem and runbook draft
content:
TL;DR: On 2025-10-31 we observed a multi-region serving degradation caused by a rare priority inversion between continuous-batching worker threads and the KV-cache maintenance loop. Symptoms: intermittent long tail latency spikes (10s of seconds), transient OOMs on small-model hosts, and request stalls that looked like deadlocks. Immediate mitigations (rate-limit routing, restart affected pools) reduced customer impact within 18 minutes. Root cause: high-priority batching jobs held per-shard mutexes while waiting on slow I/O to a cached object; maintenance tasks that needed the same mutex were blocked and could not free up evicted KV entries, which increased memory pressure and caused continuous-batching to queue more tokens, amplifying the problem into host-level OOMs.

Impact summary:
- Incident window: 2025-10-31 02:47 UTC -> 2025-10-31 03:30 UTC (containment at ~03:05 UTC, full recovery by 03:30 UTC)
- Affected tenants: ~12 hosted-api customers experiencing latency >5s; 3 dedicated pools saw transient OOM restarts
- Error class: stalled generation requests, 502/504s, and host reboots from OOM killer
- Business impact: elevated support load; a handful of API calls retried by customers; no data loss reported

Detection and signals:
- Pager triggered from tail-latency SLO alert (p50 fine, p99 spike) at 02:48 UTC
- SRE oncall noticed repeated stack traces in /var/log/runtime/worker.log indicating threads stuck in "batch_wait_for_kv" and "kv_eviction_sync"
- Metrics: per-host memory usage climbing while free-kv-entries metric dropped to near zero; batching_queue_length grew by 4x
- Traces: distributed traces showed requests waiting >10s inside batching worker before token emission

Short timeline (relevant highlights):
- 02:47 UTC: First p99 alert fired for generation latency in us-east-1
- 02:49 UTC: Oncall A (David K) SSH’ed into a representative host, saw many threads in mutex wait state and core dump from OOM on host rwr-34
- 02:52 UTC: Enabled emergency route-control policy to divert new low-priority traffic to smaller-capacity pools (reduced load on affected hosts)
- 02:56 UTC: Started rolling restart of a subset of affected hosts to clear KV state while engineers investigated
- 03:05 UTC: Eviction tuning (force-evict command) executed on affected shards to reclaim memory; p99 latency dropped substantially
- 03:30 UTC: Monitoring indicates stable memory and batching queue metrics; incident declared recovered

Root cause analysis (why it happened):
- Continuous batching workers take per-shard mutex A when assembling requests; while holding A they may issue read access to KV cache which can block on a slow decompression path (rarely observed for some cached artifacts)
- KV maintenance/eviction path requires mutex A to remove/compact entries; under normal load maintenance runs periodically and keeps free entries available
- Under a specific workload mix (many small, low-priority requests that thrash cache entries) batching workers accumulated queued tokens while holding mutex A and waiting on I/O. This prevented maintenance from running, reducing free-kv-entries and increasing memory pressure
- Memory pressure caused hosts to OOM; OOM events killed several maintenance threads and left KV maps in partially-consistent states, increasing mutex contention and creating apparent deadlocks where both batching and maintenance waited on each other
- Contributing factors:
  - No prioritized preemption: batching workers held critical mutex while doing blocking I/O
  - Eviction heuristics assumed timely maintenance runs; they did not account for mutex-holding batchers
  - Monitoring lacked a direct signal for "mutex hold times" and per-shard eviction queue depth

Why previous mitigations didn't stop it earlier:
- Autoscaling added capacity but new hosts attached to the same shard mapping and inherited the same KV state pressure
- Restarting single hosts only temporarily relieved memory pressure; without addressing the mutex inversion pattern the problem re-appeared when load converged again

Immediate actions taken (what we did during incident):
- Emergency traffic shaping to deprioritize experimental workloads
- Rolling restarts for a fraction of the pool to break the stuck mutexes and clear inconsistent KV state
- Manual forced-evict on several high-pressure shards to reclaim memory
- Temporary reduce of batching window size from 64->32 for affected capacity class to reduce per-worker lock hold time
- Post-incident: opened Linear ticket INF-2453 for full fix and tracking

Proposed permanent fixes (short term and medium term):
1) Short-term (next 2 weeks):
   - Add a mutex-hold-time metric and a p99 alert for hold >200ms
   - Change batching code to avoid holding shard mutex across blocking I/O: snapshot pointers needed for KV reads and release mutex before decompressing
   - Guard maintenance with a separate eviction token that can preempt long-held batchers (cooperative preemption)
   - Make forced-evict API callable from console for SREs with proper safety checks
2) Medium-term (1–2 months):
   - Rework eviction heuristics to account for concurrent batching pressure and implement backpressure to clients when eviction cannot free memory quickly
   - Add prioritized scheduling in the worker pool so maintenance tasks have a minimal reservation of CPU/IO
   - Add fuzz tests and chaos scenarios simulating high-thrashing small-request workloads to catch priority inversions in CI
3) Long-term (quarterly):
   - Consider moving to lock-free shard-access for read-paths and adopt generation counters for safe, wait-free KV reads
   - Explore offloading heavy decompression to isolated io-workers to keep critical mutexes uncontended

Runbook draft (for oncall):
- Detection signals:
  - p99-gen-latency > 3s AND free-kv-entries < 300 per shard for 2 minutes
  - mutex_hold_time_p99 > 200ms (after metric rollout)
  - repeated OOM events on generation hosts
- Immediate steps:
  1. Route-control: apply low-priority drop policy for non-customer-critical traffic to reduce load
  2. Scale horizontally with new pool mapping to avoid concentrating shards on same hosts
  3. If memory pressure persists: run force-evict --shard <id> for top 5 shards showing highest eviction_age
  4. If many hosts are OOMing: enable emergency rolling-restart group with staggered delays (do not reboot whole pool simultaneously)
  5. Reduce batching_window for affected capacity class to 50% as temporary mitigation
- Escalation:
  - If after 20 minutes of mitigations p99 latency not improving, page Eng-Serving-Runtime and Product-Host-API

Open action items (owners and ETA):
- [Priya] Implement mutex-hold-time metric + dashboard (ETA: 2025-11-07)
- [David K] Modify batching code to release shard mutex before heavy KV read decompression (ETA: 2025-11-14)
- [Ava M] Add forced-evict console command and safe-guards (ETA: 2025-11-10)
- [Michael O] Add CI fuzz scenario and performance test (ETA: 2025-11-30)
- [Li Wei] Draft follow-up customer incident notes for CS with mitigation summary (ETA: 2025-11-05)

Notes / things we want to capture for post-incident review meeting:
- Walk through stack traces and annotate places where mutex_A is held across I/O
- Review memory allocator behavior under high-thrash small-request loads
- Determine if any model variants produce disproportionately large decompressed cache objects (edge case)
- Confirm that eviction force-evict does not leave stale pointers (addressed in PR #891)

Appendix (quick debugging commands and artifacts saved):
- grep -n "batch_wait_for_kv" /var/log/runtime/worker.log | head
- perf top snapshot saved to /var/log/ci/perf/2025-10-31-batch-inv-sample.data
- Core dump rwr-34-core-20251031.gz (uploaded to s3://redwood-cores/incidents/2025-10-31/)
- Linear: INF-2453 (record of tasks and patches)
- GH PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/891 (eviction hardening and forced-evict API)

Quick follow-up (today): schedule 30m postmortem sync with Eng-Serving-Runtime + SRE + DX to review runbook and rollout plan for the metrics (propose 2025-11-04 16:00 UTC).

Notes to self (informal):
- This one felt like a subtle scheduling bug rather than purely memory accounting. prioritize small isolated fixes to avoid wide churn. keep the forced-evict tool behind a flag until we've got telemetry.
